segments.text: Afternoon. Mr Rutherford, is it? Gordon Rutherford?
That's me, yes. Gordon. Although the girl at the desk called me Gerald, so you never know. Is this my chair? Lovely. Terrible parking round here, isn't it?
It is, I'm afraid. And who have you brought with you?
Ravi, I'm Gordon's carer. I'm with him during the week, since he came home.
Good. And Nurse Kelly is sitting in with us too, to keep me straight on the paperwork.
Hello, Mr Rutherford. I've got your repeat prescription list here for when we need it.
So this is a check-up on how you're getting on since the stent. How have you been in yourself?

Oh, very well, very well. Better than I've any right to be. I'm back in the garden, you know, the sweet peas are up, although the slugs... my daughter says I should try that copper tape. Where was I? Yes. Fine.
I'm glad about the garden. So you feel well. Is anything at all bothering you, even something small?
Well, I do get a bit breathless going up the hill from the bus stop. Not in the flat, mind, just the hill. It's steeper than it looks. And my bus pass has stopped working, that's another thing.
Let's stay with the hill for a second. How far up are you before you notice it?
Oh, about halfway. I stop at the postbox and pretend to read the collection times.
Very wise, postboxes are excellent for that. Does it ease once you've stopped?
Straight away, it's gone in a minute. Though I did get this funny bruise on my arm, look, and I didn't bang it on anything. Ravi says I bruise like a peach.
He does. He only has to lean on a table.
Thank you for showing me. Bruises do come up easily with the sort of tablets you're on. Is it new since you came home?
Since coming home, yes. Mostly my forearms.
Now the important question. Any tightness in your chest, on that hill or sitting still?
No, nothing like that. No tightness at all. My father had a heart attack at fifty-two, you know, that's what got me to the GP in the first place.
That's useful to know, thank you. And any dizzy spells, or the room going round when you stand up?
None of that. Steady as a rock, ask Ravi.
Good. Right, the tablets are the main job today. Nurse, would you read out what we have on the list?
Of course. Clopidogrel 75 milligrams once a day, atorvastatin 80 milligrams at night, and ramipril 5 milligrams in the morning.
That's right, except the atorvastatin. Mine is 40 milligrams, I always say it to the pharmacist.
So the list says 80 milligrams of atorvastatin and Mr Rutherford says 40. Ravi, you fill the organiser. Which is it?
I fill it from the boxes and I honestly couldn't tell you offhand. I'd have to look at the label at home.
Fair enough. Please bring the box with you next time and we'll settle it then. Is the rest of the list right? Clopidogrel once a day, ramipril in the morning?
Yes, yes. Clopidogrel with my breakfast. And the ramipril too, that's for the high blood pressure I've had for twenty years. I take the two together, it's easier.

Good. Let me say that back so we're sure. Clopidogrel once a day, ramipril in the morning, and the atorvastatin dose we're still pinning down. The clopidogrel is there to keep the stent open, so that is the one you must never skip, even when the bruises are a nuisance.
I wouldn't skip it. My neighbour skipped his and ended up in hospital. Well, I think it was something else with him actually, his hip.

That sounds like a different story, but you've got the right attitude. Now, about the hill. I can't rule out that it's just lost fitness from weeks of taking it easy, so I'd like to see how it behaves over the next while.
Fitness. Yes. I did stop the walking when the weather turned. The dog doesn't like rain either, she's a spaniel.
Then the spaniel is your new personal trainer. A little more walking each day, building up slowly, and stopping at postboxes is allowed.
I'll take them both out after lunch. I'd enjoy that.
Splendid. I'd like to see you again in six weeks, to hear how the hill is treating you and to get that atorvastatin dose sorted properly.
Six weeks. Will that be before or after my sister's visit? She comes at the end of the month.
The nurse will find you a date that fits around her. Six weeks from today is the aim.
I'll book that at the desk with you on your way out, Mr Rutherford.
Lovely. Oh, and the bus pass, I nearly forgot to ask.
That one I can't help with, I'm afraid, it's the council. The desk might have their number.
Typical.
I'll ring them for you tomorrow, Gordon.
Well, I think that's everything. Anything else burning a hole in your pocket?
No, I think I've said it all. Thank you, doctor.
Goodbye for now, Mr Rutherford. Mind that hill.
